en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Bhojanavagga 33.
The Training Rule on Successive Eating.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Vesālī in the Great Forest, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, a rotation for fine meals had been established in Vesālī.
Then, it occurred to a certain poor laborer: “This cannot be an ordinary matter, since these people are preparing the meal so respectfully; what if I were to prepare a meal as well?”

Then that poor laborer approached the merchant Kirapatika; having approached him, he said this to the merchant Kirapatika: “I wish, noble sir, to provide a meal for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Give me my wages.
And that merchant Kirapatika was also faithful and confident.
Then that master of the estate gave that poor laborer an exceptionally large wage.

Thereupon, that poor laborer approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that poor laborer said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, accept my meal tomorrow."
“The community of monks is large, friend; you should know this.
“Let it be so, venerable sir, that the community of monks is large.
I have prepared many jujube fruits, and my drink mixed with jujube will be sufficient.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then that poor laborer, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
The monks heard: “It seems the poor laborer has invited the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, for tomorrow; they will be filled with drinks mixed with jujube fruit.”
Having gone for alms early in the morning, they ate.
People heard that the community of monks headed by the Buddha had been invited by a poor laborer. They brought a great abundance of hard and soft food to the poor laborer.
Then, at the end of that night, the poor laborer had exquisite hard and soft food prepared and had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, Bhante; the meal is ready.”
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of that poor laborer.
Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then that poor laborer was serving the food to the monks in the dining hall. The monks said this:
“Give a little, friend; give a little, friend.
“Venerable sirs, do not receive it little by little thinking, ‘This is a poor laborer.
Abundant food, both hard and soft, has been prepared for me.”
“Venerable sir, please accept as much as you require.
“Friend, it is not for this reason that we accept little by little.
Rather, we have already gone for alms early in the morning and eaten; therefore, we accept little by little.”
Then that poor laborer complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can it be that the venerable ones, having been invited by me, will eat elsewhere?
And I am not capable of giving as much as they require."
The monks heard that poor laborer complaining, grumbling, and carping.
Those monks who were of few desires... [they] complained, grumbled, and carp[ed]:
"How can monks, having been invited elsewhere, eat elsewhere?"... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that monks, having been invited elsewhere, eat elsewhere?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
"How indeed, monks, could those foolish men, having been invited elsewhere, eat elsewhere?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“‘Eating in succession is an offense entailing expiation’—
thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was ill.”
A certain bhikkhu, having taken almsfood, approached that bhikkhu and said to him, “Eat, friend.
“Enough, friend; I have an expectation of food,” he replied.
That bhikkhu’s almsfood was brought to him after the sun had set, and so that bhikkhu did not eat it to his heart’s content.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, for a sick bhikkhu to eat successive meals.”
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
“In eating by succession, except at the proper time, there is an offense of expiation.
Herein, this is the proper time: the time of illness—this is the proper time therein.”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, people, having prepared meals together with robes on the occasion of giving robes, invited the bhikkhus, saying, “Having fed you, we shall clothe you with robes.
The bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept, thinking, “Successive eating has been prohibited by the Blessed One.”
"A robe-material arises that is insufficient.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, to eat in succession on the occasion of giving robes."
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“In eating in succession, except at the proper time, there is an offense of expiation.
Herein, this is the proper time: the time of illness, the time of giving robes—this is the proper time therein.”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
Now at that time, people invited bhikkhus who were making robes to a meal.
The bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept, thinking, “The Blessed One has prohibited eating in succession.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
“Eating in succession, except on an appropriate occasion, is an offense entailing expiation.
Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the occasion of illness, the occasion of the distribution of robes, the occasion of making robes—this is the appropriate occasion therein.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk, approached a certain family.
Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then those people gave food to the Blessed One and to the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda, being scrupulous, did not accept it.
“Take it, Ānanda.
“Enough, Blessed One; I have expectations for my meal.
“In that case, Ānanda, take it after making a formal assignment.”
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this connection, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to eat food by means of a transfer made in succession.
And thus, bhikkhus, should it be transferred: ‘I give my share of almsfood to [name].’”
“Successive eating” means:
having been invited with one of the five kinds of cooked food, one sets that aside and eats another of the five kinds of cooked food; this is called successive eating.
“Except on the proper occasion”: [as defined previously].
Except on an occasion.
An occasion of illness means:
one is unable to eat as much as one desires while sitting on a single seat. "On an occasion of illness" means it may be eaten.

The "robe-giving season" (*cīvaradānasamaya*) refers to the last month of the rainy season when the Kathina robe has not been spread, or the five months when the Kathina robe has been spread. One may eat [at the invitation] during what is called the "robe-giving season.
The "robe-making season" (*cīvarakārasamaya*) refers to...
When a robe is being made: "It is the time for making a robe," one may eat.
If one accepts [food] thinking, "I will eat outside of the proper time," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats in succession while perceiving it as eating in succession, except on an allowable occasion, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one eats in succession while being doubtful about it, except on an allowable occasion, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one eats in succession while not perceiving it as eating in succession, except on an allowable occasion, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If it is not a meal in succession, but one perceives it as a meal in succession, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not a meal in succession, but one is doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not a meal in succession, and one does not perceive it as a meal in succession, there is no offense.
There is no offense:
at the proper time,
or having made a formal assignment, he eats.
He eats together at two or three invitations;
he eats according to the sequence of invitations;
being invited by an entire village, he eats anywhere within that village.
If invited by an entire group, he may eat anywhere within that group;
if being invited, he says, "I will take almsfood," this applies to regular meals.
at the distribution of tickets,
on the fortnightly day,
and on the Uposatha day;
On the first day of the lunar fortnight,
there is no offense in all cases except for the five kinds of cooked food;
likewise for one who is insane.
"For the first offender":
thus ends the third training rule concerning successive meals.
